articles.title: Theories and models predicting communication channel selection: a scoping review and synthesis
articles.authors: Matthew Erxleben, Jesse Fox
articles.abstract: As communication technologies continue to diversify our media environment, it is critical to understand how and why individuals select certain channels to communicate with others (e.g., face-to-face [FtF], texting, videoconferencing). First, we provide a clear conceptualization of channel selection to distinguish it from other constructs (e.g., media selection, technology adoption). Following PRISMA guidelines, we then conducted an interdisciplinary scoping review of theories and models related to channel and media choice, reviewing 4,843 sources. We identified 73 distinct theories, models, and frameworks in our initial process. Among these, we identified 38 theories that explicitly elaborated the process of individuals’ channel selection (rather than processes such as media content selection, media planning, technology adoption, or media use) and coded their primary foci and areas of origin (e.g., organizational communication, mass communication). We offer a retrospective narrative review briefly describing each channel selection theory contextualized within their theoretical predecessors (e.g., social presence theory, uses and gratifications, diffusion of innovations). Our synthesis offers additional insights on the strengths and weaknesses of current theorizing, suggesting directions for future research. Notable deficits include a lack of explication regarding how people select multiple channels, particularly over time, and a limited number of theories derived from interpersonal communication.

articles.title: The image of journalists: Toward a theoretical framework
articles.authors: Mia Grünewald
articles.abstract: The image of journalists, despite being a key component of the journalist–audience relationship, has received little scholarly attention. Beyond the limited empirical evidence, a comprehensive theoretical framework remains absent. Most existing conceptualizations focus on either the journalists’ or the audience’s perspective, are largely confined to journalistic roles, or address the image of news media rather than journalists specifically. Additionally, they neglect the reflexive perspective of how journalists perceive the audience’s image of them. Drawing on the interdisciplinary framework of Brown et al. (2006), this article proposes a comprehensive theoretical framework that conceptualizes the image of journalists as professional self-image, desired image, perceived image, transient impression, or reputation regarding the personal, work-related, organizational, or normative characteristics of journalists. By integrating all relevant perspectives, the framework provides a theoretical basis for more nuanced empirical research on the image of journalists and its implications for the journalist–audience relationship.

articles.title: Doing journalist: Boundary markers for division, jurisdiction markers for belonging
articles.authors: Lea von den Driesch, Nina Springer, Seth C Lewis
articles.abstract: Peripheral actors are often seen as a threat to journalists’ professional status and resources. Research so far has mainly focused on journalists’ discursive responses and the use of “boundary markers.” However, audiences often struggle to recognize such distinctions. To understand the strategic efforts and successes of peripheral actors, it is necessary to examine: (1) how these actors claim jurisdiction and authority through their performances; and (2) what makes their claims persuasive to publics. Drawing on symbolic interactionist perspectives, we propose a framework that distinguishes doing journalist—in contrast to doing journalism—building on West and Zimmerman’s notion of doing gender. Both practices aim to secure ascriptions of jurisdiction and authority from audiences. We illustrate the framework’s applicability with two prominent cases—from Germany (Fabian Grischkat) and the US (V Spehar)—and suggest its broader applicability (e.g., doing scientist alongside doing science or doing artist alongside doing art).

articles.title: Banal nationalism in virtual reality: An ethnographic study of the (re)production of digital national identities in social VR based on the case of Polish users
articles.authors: Jan Waligórski
articles.abstract: The emergence of each new digital medium prompts debates about its potential to foster cosmopolitanism or reinforce new forms of nationalism. To date, social virtual reality (VR) platforms have often been portrayed through a cosmopolitan lens. This article challenges that view by demonstrating how banal nationalism is (re)produced within social VR, drawing on multi-sited ethnographic research conducted among Polish users. Polish users, navigating power inequalities in access to “global communities” in VR, (re)produce digital versions of the national homeland and its landscape, avatars of the national self, and the category of the national Other. These practices demonstrate that shared digital cultural texts – such as national games, memes, and applications – can be incorporated within nationalist discourse, giving rise to new, heterogeneous forms of national identity. Despite social VR enabling global interactions, user encounters are often framed as exchanges between individuals of distinct nationalities, which generate power inequalities among users, underscoring the need to integrate the national dimension into future VR studies.

articles.title: Designing impact in extended reality: Towards social, ethical, participatory, and transformative immersive practices
articles.authors: Carles Sora-Domenjó, Anandana Kapur
articles.abstract: Extended Reality (XR) has emerged as a transformative medium for addressing social change, yet its potential for meaningful, community-centred impact remains largely unrealised. Foundational XR scholarship on presence and behavioural change has largely assessed impact through narrow metrics that privilege individual psychological effects over social transformation. Building on contemporary frameworks of interactive documentary “i-docs,” current XR research and impact theory, this paper proposes a qualitative framework conceived as a design tool to co-design XR experiences for civic engagement, community empowerment and socio-political transformation. Precisely because impact intentions are built into the design process from the outset, the framework inherently becomes an evaluative tool, allowing teams to continuously monitor whether those intentions are being met by the final XR experience. Drawing from Sora-Domenjó and Kapur’s (2022) approach to i-docs impact—which examines how interactive and immersive technologies create pathways between individual empathy and participatory action—the paper argues that XR’s affordances require integrated design and evaluation strategies. This work highlights why understanding XR impact demands attention to both psychological and social dimensions, which we view as complementary rather than mutually exclusive. To address this, a qualitative ecosystem-oriented framework is proposed that bridges design and evaluation, grounded in six interrelated dimensions: (i) Co-creation, (ii) Community Emplacement, (iii) Meaningful Participation, (iv) Digital Community Building, (v) Technological Inclusivity and Accessibility and (vi) Cross-Media and Context Design. These dimensions align with broader XR research showing that lasting behavioural and attitudinal changes emerge not from immersion alone but from structured pre, during and post-experience reflection, activations, participatory processes, community scaffolding, and meaningful agency. By reframing XR not as an “empathy machine” but as a collaborative space for knowledge-making, this framework emphasises long-term community relationships.

articles.title: Public service programming in the age of platforms: Innovation, identity, and impact
articles.authors: Daniel Martin, Catalina Iordache, Julie Münter Lassen, Antonio Nucci, Jacek Mikucki, Katarzyna Gajlewicz-Korab
articles.abstract: Facing increased competition for audiences and content from global streaming services, public service media (PSM) organisations have increasingly prioritised ‘big statement programmes’ as a means of securing reach and relevance within on-demand environments. This article examines how PSM organisations reinterpret the value of such programmes, focussing on how individual titles are positioned as emblematic of public service missions. Drawing on a comparative thematic analysis of interviews and organisational documents related to 27 programmes across nine PSM organisations – in Belgium (Flanders and Wallonia), Denmark, Italy, Poland, and the UK – the article examines how programme-level prioritisation has become a key site of strategy and value negotiation. Across cases, we identify three sites of discursive tension between strategies and values: shifting understandings of innovation towards popular formats that can reach audiences across linear and non-linear services; differing constructions of impact that balance civic significance with reach; and contrasting interpretations of national identity shaped by market, regulatory, and cultural contexts.

articles.title: Symptom-Level Comorbidity Patterns Between Depression and Internet Gaming Disorder Among Adolescents: Evidence from Longitudinal Network Analysis with Gender Considerations
articles.authors: Shiyun Chen, Yue Zhao, Xinli Chi, Shimin Zhu
articles.abstract: Adolescence is a period with an increased risk for the co-occurrence of depression and Internet gaming disorder (IGD), yet we still know little about how specific symptoms of these two conditions influence each other over time. In this study, we applied cross-lagged panel network analysis to two-wave data from a community sample of 538 adolescents (Mean age = 12.51 years; 53.7 percent female). Potential gender differences in the network structure were examined. In the overall sample and in both gender groups, depressive symptoms consistently predicted later gaming-related problems, whereas no reverse cross-disorder pathways were retained. In particular, suicidal ideation and psychomotor symptoms emerged as bridge symptoms linking depression and IGD, while sleep problems showed moderate outgoing expected influence in the overall symptom network. While boys and girls showed broadly similar patterns, some differences emerged in how specific symptoms were connected and which symptoms were most influential. These findings clarify the longitudinal symptom-level associations between depression and IGD in adolescents, suggesting that addressing key depressive symptoms may help reduce the risk of later IGD.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and journalism in Ibero-America: A comparative study of perceptions, practices and challenges
articles.authors: Paulo Nuno Vicente, Sara Pérez-Seijo, Suzana Barbosa
articles.abstract: This article explores the perceptions, practices, challenges and opportunities associated with the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in journalistic practice within the Ibero-American context. Drawing on an original quantitative comparative study conducted in Portugal, Spain and Brazil, the research investigates how professional journalists understand, engage with and respond to the integration of AI-driven tools in newsrooms. Based on survey data from 271 journalists, the findings reveal widespread but predominantly basic knowledge of AI, general curiosity and cautious optimism regarding its implementation, and notable concern about its impact on professional ethics, job security, and editorial transparency. The study highlights significant variations across countries in the use of AI applications. Key challenges identified include the absence of formal editorial guidelines, limited training opportunities and a lack of transparency in the use of AI-generated content. The research underscores the urgent need for institutional strategies that ensure responsible AI integration, safeguard journalistic standards and support professional development.

articles.title: Trending by design: How algorithmic activists amplified and recalibrated an elite anti-Ukrainian campaign on X
articles.authors: Piotr Marczyński
articles.abstract: The ability of far-right actors to manipulate social media traffic sparks concerns over the quality of public discourse. Although the scholarship on far-right digital activism has established its role in aiding elite communication, we know little about mechanisms through which such campaigns are amplified and recalibrated in the process. This article addresses this gap through the lens of algorithmic activism, investigating how digital activists leveraged platform features to amplify and recalibrate the elite-initiated campaign #StopUkrainizacjiPolski on X. Combining descriptive statistics, social network analysis and critical discourse analysis, we examine 130,788 posts from February 2022 to September 2024. Findings demonstrate that a small group of accounts amplified the hashtag by hijacking the X trending board while recalibrating campaign objectives via indexical linkages to other hashtags, invoking instrumental pacifism, historical grievances, and antisemitic conspiracy theories. The study elucidates how platform affordances shape how digital activists engage in elite campaigns with implications for the reach and form of exclusionary discourse.

articles.title: Diminishing returns to calibrated reliance on AI: effects on deliverable quality and rework effort, moderated by task verifiability
articles.authors: Junjie Sun, Yifan Yang, Jiangnan Cheng, Weichao Ding
articles.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can function as both “performance accelerators” and “risk propagators” in organizations. This study investigates how AI-enabled work capability, particularly employees' decomposition and evaluation skills, is associated with deliverable quality and rework effort through the behavioral pathway of calibrated reliance on AI. Additionally, it examines task verifiability as a critical boundary condition that shapes the effectiveness of human-AI collaboration. Design/methodology/approach Guided by appropriate reliance and automation trust theories, data from 380 workers were analyzed using SmartPLS 4 (partial least squares structural equation modeling) and hierarchical polynomial regression to test mediation, moderation, and quadratic effects. Procedural remedies and a latent method factor approach were employed to assess common method bias. Findings AI-enabled work capability was positively associated with calibrated reliance on AI. Calibrated reliance on AI was associated with higher deliverable quality and lower rework effort. A double diminishing marginal pattern emerged: as reliance calibration increased, quality gains and rework reductions leveled off, indicating a “too-much-of-a-good-thing” pattern. Task verifiability strengthened the positive association between calibrated reliance and deliverable quality and also strengthened its negative association with rework effort. Originality/value This study shifts the focus from reliance intensity to reliance calibration in explaining AI-enabled work outcomes. It documents a double diminishing marginal pattern, showing that the benefits of calibrated reliance are meaningful but not unlimited. It also identifies task verifiability as a boundary condition that helps explain when calibrated reliance is more strongly associated with improved deliverable quality and reduced rework effort. These findings provide focused guidance for capability development, reliance calibration, and task-specific AI governance.

articles.title: The challenge of AI dependence: exploring its impact on cognitive autonomy and elaboration in creative performance
articles.authors: Yanyang Ma, Kerun Li, Yulei Liu
articles.abstract: Purpose As artificial intelligence advances and its application scenarios continue to expand, human–artificial intelligence interaction grows increasingly close. While artificial intelligence brings convenience, it also raises concerns that it may weaken users' cognitive autonomy. To investigate this issue. This study aims to explore the composition of AI dependence and its impact on cognitive autonomy and specific aspects of creative performance. Design/methodology/approach This study draws on cognitive evaluation theory and the elaboration likelihood model to construct a dual-pathway model with instrumental dependence and affective dependence as core variables. The model explains the formation mechanisms of the two types of artificial intelligence dependence and their differential effects on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily examines their potential role in the elaboration dimension of creative performance. A two-stage mixed-method design was employed to test the model. Findings Study 1 found that perceived trust mainly had a positive effect on instrumental dependence. Different dimensions of interactivity differentially affected affective dependence and cognitive autonomy. Mediation analysis further confirmed the core mediating role of Dependence. Study 2, a small-sample exploratory experiment, re-tested selected hypotheses and found a possible negative effect of instrumental dependence on the elaboration dimension of creative performance. Research limitations/implications The main theoretical contribution of this study lies in revealing the dual-pathway formation mechanisms of artificial intelligence dependence and the reshaping effects of different types of dependence on cognitive autonomy. It also preliminarily explores the potential effects of dependence on elaboration performance. Originality/value The dual-pathway dependence model constructed in this study offers practical implications for understanding how long-term use of artificial intelligence affects cognitive autonomy.

articles.title: Understanding the enacted behaviors of university students susceptible to cybersecurity risks: a community of practice perspective
articles.authors: Maharazu Kasim, Anup Shrestha, Samuel C. Avemaria Utulu
articles.abstract: Purpose Organizations carry out an ethical hacking approach to combat cybersecurity challenges, focusing on the technical aspects of cybersecurity vulnerabilities. This practice persists despite evidence that shows that human-enacted cybersecurity vulnerabilities constitute a significant threat to organizational cybersecurity. To address this challenge, we propose a socio-ethical hacking framework to deal with cybersecurity vulnerabilities in organizations. This framework shows how these behaviors are embedded in and reinforced through the everyday practices of organizational actors. Design/methodology/approach We adopted an interpretive case study research method using the community of practice (CoP) theory as the theoretical lens and university undergraduate students as the study context. Research data were collected through interviews and participatory observation. Findings The study identified how the social structure of undergraduate students shapes the enactment of behaviors that constitute cybersecurity vulnerabilities. Organizational actors jointly create social behaviors and actions that make organizations vulnerable to cybersecurity challenges. Practical implications Using this study, organizations can combine both technical ethical hacking and social ethical hacking practices to detect technical and behavioral vulnerabilities that expose their organization to cyber security threats. Social implications Organizations develop new insights on how to detect taken-for-granted enacted vulnerabilities that can surpass the best cyber security protocols put in place. Using the CoP theory, this study has established the relevance of social factors and how they can enhance understanding human vulnerability, particularly behaviors vulnerable to cybersecurity threats. Originality/value While there are numerous studies looking at the human factor in cybersecurity, there is little evidence of studies showing how these behaviors are enacted and experienced as taken-for-granted actions within their social contexts. This study enhanced studies in the human vulnerability research stream particularly as they relate to how social structure of organizational actors lead to the enactment of behaviors susceptible to a cybersecurity threat.

articles.title: The AI trust paradox: how disclosure, brand authenticity and consumer mindset shape communication effectiveness
articles.authors: George Chung-Chi Shen, Wen-Hsien Huang
articles.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the trust paradox in artificial intelligence (AI)-generated content, where efficiency conflicts with perceived inauthenticity. Integrating source credibility theory and congruity theory, it examines how the interplay between ad genesis (AI vs. genuine), strategic context (disclosure, brand authenticity) and consumer mindset (construal level) determines communication effectiveness. Design/methodology/approach A three-study experimental design was employed to isolate specific contingencies. Study 1 manipulated ad genesis and AI disclosure to test engagement. Study 2 examined the moderating role of brand authenticity on purchase intentions. Study 3 tested the congruity between AI message focus (hedonic vs. utilitarian) and consumer construal levels. Findings Genuine imagery generally outperforms AI-generated imagery; however, effectiveness is contingent on strategic fit. Disclosure boosts engagement for genuine ads but reduces it for AI content. AI ads enhance purchase intentions for low-authenticity brands but damage high-authenticity ones. Furthermore, hedonic AI appeals align with high-construal mindsets, whereas utilitarian appeals suit low-construal consumers. Research limitations/implications The experiments used static images in controlled online settings. Future research should test dynamic and multimodal AI content and validate the effects with real-world behavioral metrics, such as click-through and conversion rates. Practical implications AI use should fit the context. Heritage brands should avoid AI imagery, whereas challenger brands can benefit from it. Disclosure helps genuine-image ads but hurts AI-generated ads. Hedonic AI appeals suit abstract mindsets, whereas utilitarian appeals suit concrete mindsets. Originality/value This research advances advertising theory by applying a split-credibility lens to AI-generated advertising, demonstrating that effectiveness depends on source-context congruence.

articles.title: Balancing efficiency and responsibility in generative AI adoption
articles.authors: Duy Khanh Phan, Bao Quoc Truong-Dinh, Em Thi Diem Nguyen
articles.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how firms achieve sustainable outcomes from generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) adoption by balancing efficiency gains with ethical and environmental responsibilities. It integrates dynamic capability theory and responsible AI governance to examine the mediating role of digital dynamic capability (DsDC) and the moderating effect of responsible AI orientation (RAIO). Design/methodology/approach Two complementary empirical studies were undertaken. Study 1 applies a staggered difference-in-differences design with propensity-score matching (DiD-PSM) to 500 GenAI adoption events (2019–2024). Study 2 employs a two-step system generalised method of moments (GMM) estimator for 1,274 firm-year observations (2016–2024) to analyse persistence, mediation and moderation effects. Findings GenAI adoption was associated with a market-perceived efficiency signal (a 2.7% rise in cumulative abnormal returns) alongside a 1.9% decline in environmental, social and governance sentiment, a reputational rather than substantive sustainability indicator, evidencing an efficiency-responsibility tension. Over time, DDC helped partially translate these short-term gains into sustainable performance, while RAIO mitigated ethical and reputational risks, enhancing firms’ long-term legitimacy. Research limitations/implications The study relies on archival indicators and text-derived governance measures; future research could combine these data with surveys or internal audit evidence. Practical implications Managers should pair GenAI deployment with adaptive digital capability and responsible AI governance to protect stakeholder trust. Originality/value This study advances theory by integrating capability and governance perspectives to explain the sustainability of GenAI adoption. Methodologically, it introduces temporal triangulation by combining DiD-PSM and System GMM, offering a novel dynamic causal framework for responsible digital transformation.

articles.title: Concurrent and Longitudinal Associations Between Childhood Trauma, Attachment and Relationship Satisfaction in Couples
articles.authors: Noémie Bigras, Natalie O. Rosen, Alice Girouard, E. Sandra Byers, Katherine Péloquin, Sophie Bergeron
articles.abstract: Objective This longitudinal study examined the dyadic associations between childhood trauma (CT) and relationship satisfaction, and the role of attachment insecurity therein. Background CT is a known risk factor for couple dissatisfaction. One conceptual framework that may explain this association is attachment theory, which suggests that abusive or neglectful primary caregivers in childhood contribute to the development of insecure adult attachment and in turn, to lower romantic relationship satisfaction. Yet past studies examining the role of CT in adult couple relationships have primarily used cross-sectional and individual-level designs, limiting our understanding of how CT influences couples’ relationship satisfaction over time. Method A convenience sample of 210 heterosexual cisgender and sexually/gender diverse community couples (M age = 31 years old, SD = 8.50) completed online questionnaires at three time points (baseline, 6 months and 12 months) over one year. Based on the Actor-Partner Independence Model, cross-sectional and longitudinal mediation models were conducted. Results A person’s greater history of CT was linked to both their own and their partner’s lower relationship satisfaction concurrently and with their own lower relationship satisfaction 12 months later. Attachment anxiety was a significant mediator of these associations. Conclusion Results highlight the contribution of attachment anxiety as a central mechanism to couples’ relationship satisfaction in the aftermath of CT. They also underscore the enduring influence of distal interpersonal vulnerabilities on proximal relational outcomes via their expression in adult attachment dynamics, supporting the need for attachment- and trauma-informed care.

articles.title: Compassionate and Self-Critical Self-Relating Following Interpersonal Trauma: Differential Associations With Cognitive Emotion Regulation and Interpersonal Competence
articles.authors: Huiyoung Shin, Yu-Jin An
articles.abstract: Interpersonal trauma poses enduring challenges for relational functioning in early adulthood, yet substantial heterogeneity exists in how individuals adapt interpersonally following such experiences. Drawing on self-compassion theory and emotion-regulation flexibility perspectives, this study examined how self-compassion—conceptualized as a multidimensional construct comprising positive (self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness) and negative (self-judgment, isolation, over-identification) components—relates to interpersonal competence, and whether adaptive and maladaptive cognitive emotion-regulation strategies differentially accounted for these associations. Participants were 1,004 South Korean young adults (49.8% male; M age = 29.47) who had experienced a subjectively distressing interpersonal event or relational loss. They completed measures of self-compassion, cognitive emotion regulation, and interpersonal competence. Path-analytic models examined direct and indirect associations among these variables. Additional moderation analyses examined whether the associations between self-compassion and cognitive emotion regulation differed by sex. Overall self-compassion was positively associated with interpersonal competence, with this association driven primarily by positive components of self-compassion. Positive components of self-compassion exhibited robust indirect associations with interpersonal competence via greater use of adaptive cognitive emotion-regulation strategies (e.g., acceptance, positive reappraisal). In contrast, negative components of self-compassion were associated with reduced use of adaptive strategies and greater use of maladaptive strategies (e.g., rumination, self-blame). Negative components also showed small positive indirect associations with interpersonal competence through maladaptive strategies, suggesting that these strategies were not uniformly associated with lower interpersonal competence. Tests of moderation by sex showed that the associations between self-compassion and cognitive emotion regulation were largely comparable across male and female participants. Together, these findings suggest that individual differences in self-relating and cognitive emotion regulation may help explain heterogeneity in interpersonal competence and are broadly consistent with emotion-regulation flexibility perspectives on adaptation following interpersonal trauma.

articles.title: Peer Neglect, Maladaptive Self-Cognition, and Adolescent Somatic Symptoms: A Cross-Lagged Panel Analysis
articles.authors: Sen Li, Ruosi Gao, Xuejiao Li, Fengjing Zhang, Ningning Gong, Jing Chen, Shuo Xu, Shufen Xing
articles.abstract: Somatic symptoms refer to physical discomforts that cannot be fully explained by organic or physiological causes. Drawing on social pain theory, stress generation theory, and cognitive theory, peer neglect may be associated with maladaptive self-cognition, thereby increasing vulnerability to somatic symptoms. In turn, drawing on labeling theory, adolescents with somatic symptoms may be more likely to experience peer neglect through social labeling processes. The present study aimed to test the bidirectional relationships among peer neglect, maladaptive self-cognition, and somatic symptoms, examine the mediating role of maladaptive self-cognition in the relation between peer neglect and somatic symptoms, and explore whether these associations differed by gender. A cross-lagged panel model was used to analyze data from 1639 Chinese adolescents (52.50% girls, M age = 14.52 years, SD = 1.08; 47.50% boys, M age = 14.45 years, SD = 1.15 at baseline) recruited through convenience sampling. Data were collected across two measurement waves over a seven-month period. The findings revealed reciprocal longitudinal associations between peer neglect and somatic symptoms. Maladaptive self-cognition showed a small indirect effect in the association between peer neglect and subsequent somatic symptoms, whereas no significant gender differences were found. These findings suggest that maladaptive self-cognition may represent one possible psychological pathway linking peer neglect to somatic symptoms. Peer neglect and maladaptive self-cognition may therefore be relevant areas for future school-based intervention research.

articles.title: Hidden, Yet Pervasive: Social Inequality in Journalism (Research)
articles.authors: Andreas A. Riedl, Thomas Hanitzsch, Thomas R. Schmidt, Nik Usher
articles.abstract: Social inequality is a defining feature of contemporary societies and a major driver of political polarization. In deeply mediatized contexts, journalism occupies a pivotal position: It shapes discourses on inequality while simultaneously being structured by unequal distributions of resources, power, and recognition. In this conceptual essay, we propose a taxonomy based on four inequality arenas— top-bottom , us-them , inside-outside , and today-tomorrow inequalities. These arenas intersect with three areas of study—inequality mediated by journalism, within journalism, and in journalism research. In so doing, we offer an analytical roadmap that highlights central tensions, persistent shortcomings, and potential future research priorities in the field.

articles.title: The Political Leaning of Fact-Checking: Countering Italian Disinformation on the War in Ukraine
articles.authors: Tommaso Valastro, Sergio Splendore
articles.abstract: The intense disinformation efforts that accompanied Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine highlight the importance of countering misinformation to mitigate the influence of foreign actors, particularly in vulnerable public spheres such as the Italian one. Despite widespread use, the effectiveness of fact-checking in correcting misinformation remains ambiguous, with limited exploration of the underlying reasons. This article focuses on the role of political leaning and partisanship in shaping individuals’ comprehension of factual information, their inclination to fact-checking exposure, and their capacity to assimilate findings that challenge their preconceived beliefs. We measure the role of these variables for 10 different statements about Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, employing original survey data collected in Italy in spring 2022. We find veracity assessment to be associated with partisan views of the war for both true and false statements, with Russia-leaning views frequently correlating with lower exposure to and reception of fact-checks. Right-leaning political attitudes often work in the same direction, in some cases amplifying the partisan rejection of fact-checks. These findings contribute to literature on fact-checking, selective exposure, motivated reasoning, and misinformation, corroborating previous studies on the limits of debunking efforts and extending their insights to a setting well known for its high level of political parallelism. A crucial implication of these results is that political attitudes should receive greater consideration when addressing misinformation and foreign disinformation efforts, given their potential to amplify partisan barriers that moderate the corrective power of fact-checking. Furthermore, this partisan acceptance of fact-checks complicates the normative assessment of journalistic practices.

articles.title: Incompatible Interpretive Worlds: TikTok, Douyin, and Geopolitical Narratives of the Russia–Ukraine War
articles.authors: Jing Yang, Zhiyuan Liang
articles.abstract: This study compares the ways TikTok and its mainland Chinese counterpart, Douyin, have mediated the Russia–Ukraine war, generating divergent geopolitical narratives. It examines the political role of platform dissemination in contemporary warfare by analysing how platform logics and governance contexts shape public sense-making of conflict. On TikTok, war narratives emerge through creator-led circulation, cross-border viewing, translation, and comment-mediated interpretation, producing forms of transnational witnessing that are affective, participatory, and contested. In contrast, Douyin operates within the Chinese domestic discourse system, where official emphasis on neutrality, stability, and diplomatic restraint shapes its dominant interpretive framework. In the corpus, footage of frontline violence appears less consistently prominent, while explanatory narratives attributing the war to NATO expansion or Western provocation appear frequently in high-visibility content. This distribution should not be interpreted as an explicit pro-Russian diplomatic stance. Rather, it reflects the importance of sovereignty-oriented reasoning and nationalist sentiment in Chinese political communication. Drawing on comparative qualitative content analysis of high-engagement, platform-curated war-related videos retrieved through hashtag-based sampling on TikTok and Douyin, this study argues that the two applications produce incompatible interpretive worlds: one organised around transnational humanitarian witnessing and contested moral interpretation, and the other around institutionally anchored geopolitical explanation, sovereignty-oriented reasoning, and participatory nationalist uptake.

articles.title: Beyond Technological Lag: Re-Centering Marginalized Media Markets in Global AI Journalism
articles.authors: Mathias-Felipe De-Lima-Santos, Bruce Mutsvairo
articles.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) in journalism has been built largely on evidence from well-resourced newsrooms in Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic nations. This thematic issue focuses on media markets that are marginalized economically, politically, linguistically, or epistemically. Its 17 articles examine newsrooms, journalists, educators, developers, and public discourse across Sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Europe, Latin America, BRICS (an international group currently comprising 10 countries: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates), and the Caribbean. Read together, these studies show that AI adoption at the margins is selective, bounded, and human-gated, shaped by subscription costs, scarce local data, missing newsroom policies, state agendas, and dependence on platforms built elsewhere. Journalists respond with layered boundary work and what contributors call “defensive” forms of governance, protecting verification, judgement, and accountability as human domains. The issue also shows that AI is made meaningful through discourse before it is experienced, as hype, risk narratives, and representations position marginalized societies as recipients rather than co-producers of AI futures. We argue that marginality is relational and that it changes what AI does to journalism. We close with an agenda for comparative, locally grounded, and decolonial research on AI and news.

articles.title: TikTok as a Site for Ethno-Political Contestations and Conflict Mediation Among Ethiopian Diaspora
articles.authors: Abdissa Zerai, Gizachew Nemomsa
articles.abstract: This study examines how TikTok has served as a site for both ethno-political contestations and conflict mediation in the context of Ethiopia by focusing on the engagement of the Ethiopian diasporic community on the platform. Informed by the deliberative democratic theoretical framework, it addresses how ethno-political contestations among the diasporic community discursively manifest themselves in the TikTok sphere and how such diasporic community mediates the contestations on the platform. In addressing these, critical discourse analysis was employed on purposively selected TikTok content created from October 2023 to September 2024 across four key thematic areas. The findings indicate that the ethno-political contestations among the diasporic community manifested themselves on the TikTok sphere by juxtaposing exclusionary ethnic identity against inclusive pan-Ethiopian identity. Such contestations were enacted through the deployment of charged rhetoric. However, the contestations were mediated by pushing back against destructive discursive trends through strategic intervention of some TikTok hosts. The platform served as a site for both an ideological battlefield and a counter-platform for challenging polemical discourses and for promoting deliberative discourse among the Ethiopian diaspora. Contrary to the prevailing skepticism about TikTok’s potential for meaningful discourse, this study reveals that if deployed strategically, it can be a valuable platform for advancing rational dialogue among disparate groups, which could be instrumental in encouraging participants to seek collective solutions for enduring political problems.

articles.title: The science of beauty: Looksmaxxing, self-help, and genetic fatalism in women’s online spaces
articles.authors: Rachel Bergmann, Elizabeth Fetterolf
articles.abstract: This paper examines the emergence of “looksmaxxing” in women’s online spaces. As a specific and underexamined element within what Jilly Boyce Kay analyzes as “reactionary feminism,” essentialist logics about gender and race are operationalized through the aesthetics of science and self-optimization rather than explicitly political rhetoric. Users construct the “science of beauty” through decentralized forms of expertise, from plastic surgery influencers to scientific racism to community-generated aesthetic taxonomies. We identify a thread of individualized and intimate genetic fatalism shaping both aesthetic frameworks and the tactics used to achieve them, mutating the postfeminist promise of self-transformation toward distinctly reactionary goals. This tension between the essentialism and malleability of the body makes the paradigm generative and self-sustaining, absorbing failure and keeping users invested. This case is a call to examine “fringe” and aesthetics-focused cultural formations for insight on how bioessentialist ideas about race and gender circulate today.

articles.title: When availability is not enough: Content prominence and diversity on a public service VoD platform
articles.authors: Raul Lobanov
articles.abstract: As public service media (PSM) shift from broadcasting to video on demand (VoD), prominence has become a key mechanism through which public value is operationalised. While policy debates emphasise the visibility of culturally significant content, evidence on how interface prominence shapes viewing remains scarce. Building on theories of affordances, prominence, and media diversity, this article conceptualises diversity transformation as the process through which diversity changes from catalogue availability, through interface prominence, to audience consumption. Using a longitudinal dataset from Estonian Public Broadcasting (ERR), the study finds that prominence and premieres are the strongest predictors of VoD viewing, explaining 62 per cent of the variance. The findings illustrate a process of diversity transformation: Although ERR’s VoD catalogue is diverse, interface prominence and audience consumption become concentrated around scripted and foreign titles. The study confirms that the VoD interface has become a strategic site where PSM negotiate tensions between universality, cultural responsibility, and audience demand.

articles.title: The Associations Between Depressive Symptoms, Excessive Reassurance‐Seeking, and the Quality of Romantic Relationships in Young Adult Couples: A Dyadic Longitudinal Mediation Model
articles.authors: Fatmawati Fadli, Nicholas J. Moberly, Lamprini Psychogiou
articles.abstract: This study used a dyadic mediation model to examine actor and partner effects in the associations between depressive symptoms and the quality of romantic relationships, both directly and indirectly via excessive reassurance‐seeking. A total of 105 heterosexual young adult couples participated in a three‐wave longitudinal study (waves 1‐month apart) through the Prolific platform. Participants completed measures of depressive symptoms, excessive reassurance‐seeking, and multiple dimensions of romantic relationship qualities at each time point. After controlling for autoregressive and reciprocal effects, several direct and indirect actor and partner effects emerged. Direct actor effects were only significant for men (not women), showing that when men reported higher depressive symptoms at Time 1, they experienced greater companionship, intimate disclosure, and emotional support at Time 3. Direct partner effects were significant for both women and men, indicating that when women reported higher depressive symptoms at Time 1, their partners experienced less companionship and satisfaction at Time 3. However, when men reported higher depressive symptoms at Time 1, their partners reported receiving less criticism at Time 3. In terms of indirect effects, depressive symptoms in men at Time 1 predicted their higher reassurance‐seeking at Time 2, which, in turn, predicted increased partners' perceptions of being criticized and excluded at Time 3 (actor–partner effects). Conversely, depressive symptoms in women at Time 1 predicted higher partners' reassurance‐seeking at Time 2, which, in turn, predicted decreased women's perceptions of being criticized and excluded at Time 3 (partner–partner effects). These findings highlight the complex interpersonal dynamics of depressive symptoms in young adult romantic relationships and suggest that men's excessive reassurance‐seeking may be one potential pathway linking individuals' depressive symptoms with their own and their partners' perceptions and behaviors within romantic relationships.

articles.title: Joke's On You: A Social Relations Analysis of Humor Styles in Friendships
articles.authors: Irene J. Kim, Lily Unger, Hyewon Yang, Mariah F. Purol, William J. Chopik
articles.abstract: Humor plays an important role in the formation and maintenance of close relationships, yet little is known about how people come to perceive their friends as funny or as using different humor styles. The present study examined perceptions of funniness and humor styles in 185 naturally occurring friendship groups ( N = 740). In the context of the Social Relations Model, friends demonstrated modest consensus regarding humor styles and funniness, indicating that humor is sufficiently observable to generate shared impressions. At the same time, substantial perceiver and relationship variances suggested that humor judgments are also shaped by individual tendencies and the unique dynamics of particular friendships. Self‐other agreement and assumed similarity were also evident across humor styles. Finally, adaptive humor styles and general funniness were associated with greater friendship satisfaction, while aggressive and self‐defeating humor were associated with poorer friendship quality. These findings position humor as both an individual characteristic and an interpersonal perception that emerges through close relationships.

articles.title: Rasch Analysis of the Korean Internet Social Capital Scales
articles.authors: Kyeongwon Lee
articles.abstract: Internet‐based ties increasingly function as social resources, but item‐ and category‐level evidence for the Korean Internet Social Capital Scales (K‐ISCS) remains limited. This study evaluated the 18‐item, 7‐point K‐ISCS using Rasch measurement in a nationwide online panel of Korean adults ( n = 1500). Residual‐based dimensionality diagnostics supported the theoretical distinction between online bonding and bridging social capital; therefore, the main analyses were conducted separately by subscale. Both subscales showed generally acceptable item fit, ordered category functioning, high person reliability and separation, and precisely estimated item difficulty hierarchies within the calibration sample. Item 4 in the bonding subscale and item 18 in the bridging subscale showed underfit, indicating the need for closer review of the emergency‐loan and frequent‐new‐contact items. Person–item maps and test information functions showed that both subscales measured most precisely near the center of the latent continuum, with lower precision at the tails. DIF was mostly negligible across gender and age groups, although item 18 showed slight‐to‐moderate gender‐related DIF. Overall, the findings support interpreting the K‐ISCS as two related but distinct subscales for assessing perceived online bonding and bridging resources in Korean adults, rather than as an undifferentiated total score.

articles.title: The Theory of Rhythmic Synergy in Caregiving for Older Adults Living With Dementia
articles.authors: Chloe E. Gonzales, Tamara D. Afifi, Andy J. Merolla
articles.abstract: This manuscript sets forth a theory of rhythmic synergy to depict the dynamic and adaptive process of communication and sensemaking that caregivers experience when caring for someone living with dementia. The theory emerged from in‐depth, semi‐structured interviews with 31 adult family caregivers of a person living with dementia. Rhythmic synergy refers to a higher‐order, relationally entrained state in which the caregiver perceives an implicit knowing of their person living with dementia and how to interact with them. It is developed over time through a process where the caregiver iteratively responds to the person living with dementia and strategically engages in adapting their verbal and nonverbal communication behaviors (i.e., rhythms) and sensing a kind of togetherness or presence (i.e., relational synergy) that fosters positive outcomes for the caregiver and person living with dementia. The theory also addresses the ways in which members of a care partner network can enhance or disrupt the process of developing rhythmic synergy. Importantly, the theory helps explain how temporality is crucial in understanding communication in dementia caregiving, including symptom progression, increasing care demands, and changes in the network of care partners over time.

articles.title: Tears for Better, for Worse: Typology and Measure of Crying in Romantic Relationships
articles.authors: Adrianna Kaczuba‐Kozic, Karolina Koszałkowska, Monika Wróbel
articles.abstract: People typically cry in the presence of their romantic partners, yet the social functions of this behavior within couples remain unknown. Drawing on the social glue model of tears and prior research on manipulative crying, we identified five distinct types of crying in romantic relationships and created the Crying in Romantic Relationships Questionnaire (CRRQ) to measure them. The CRRQ was developed and validated across three studies in Polish and UK samples ( N = 849). In the Preliminary Study, individuals described real‐life situations in which people might cry in the presence of their partners. Based on their answers, we created an initial item pool. Study 1 examined the psychometric properties of the pool, revealing that the CRRQ comprises five factors, each representing a different type of crying: relationship discomfort, relationship comfort, other‐oriented concern, emotion regulation, and manipulation. The results also supported the scale's reliability and validity. Study 2 provided further evidence for the five‐dimensional structure of the CRRQ and its good psychometric properties. Overall, the results indicate that the CRRQ is a reliable and valid measure of five distinct types of crying in romantic relationships.

articles.title: Discursive constructions of epistemic authority and boundary-work in a state-sponsored Turkish popular science magazine
articles.authors: Osman Aksit, Ulku Seher Budak
articles.abstract: This study examined the discursive construction of epistemic authority of science in a state-supported popular science magazine, in the face of the challenges posed by the post-truth era. The research analyzed how science constructs and negotiates legitimacy through boundary-work and expertise typologies within the relationship among scientists, the state, and citizens. The magazine’s discourse appeared to reinforce scientific certainty and privilege through institutional authorization, methodological rationalization, and state–science alignment. The findings showed science integrated into the national narrative is positioned beyond a technical field as a vehicle for moral and collective responsibility. This reveals a multi-layered legitimization process where the magazine negotiates political priorities while preserving autonomy.

articles.title: Fandom Rupture in the Movement Society: Reactive Collective Participation Through Affective Practices
articles.authors: Zhihong Li
articles.abstract: When an external shock draws heterogeneous actors into a single platform arena before any collective aim emerges, participation persists at movement-like intensity. Existing theories have not specified the cohering mechanism through which this formation sustains. This study conceptualizes this mode as reactive collective participation and specifies how affective publics cohere and persist under reactive conditions at the practice level. A mixed-methods design integrates in-depth interviews with 13 heterogeneously positioned participants (fans, anti-fans, bystanders) and computational analysis of Weibo discourse surrounding the 2023 Cai Xukun scandal (139,795 posts; 205,001 comments). Four affective practices recur across the event: Positioning, Storying, Attunement, and Calibration. These practices shift in relative weight across the event’s life cycle and distribute unevenly across actor positions, producing a stratified ecology in which insulated defense and exposed antagonism sustain each other. The study advances affective publics theory by specifying how affective publics cohere and persist under reactive conditions at practice level, and collective participation theory by conceptualizing reactive collective participation as a mode that reconnects the movement society and fan activism frameworks through a reactive pathway.

articles.title: Women Sustaining TikTok as Supplementary Information Infrastructure for Flexible Work Arrangements: Gendered Conditions, Community and Surveillance
articles.authors: Xuefei Li, Kiran Ijaz, Marta E. Cecchinato, Naseem Ahmadpour
articles.abstract: Flexible work arrangements (FWAs) create practical and interpretive questions that formal workplace information may not adequately address, particularly around how flexibility is experienced and negotiated in everyday working life. As workers share and encounter FWA-related posts on TikTok, the platform can provide supplementary access to experiential knowledge. However, circulation alone does not explain how such knowledge becomes a durable and usable resource for workers. Drawing on infrastructure theory, we conceptualise TikTok as a supplementary information infrastructure (SII) and use a feminist perspective to examine the gendered conditions under which women contribute to and sustain it. Based on semi-structured interviews with 14 women who post about FWAs on TikTok, we analyse their relational information practices. Participants responded to misleading information with situated knowledge and interpretive resources that made workplace norms more visible and contestable. Sustaining this infrastructure came at a cost: credibility and continued participation were shaped by gendered conditions of recognition and unequal access to time and energy, while trust was challenged by shifting audiences, limited contextualisation and technological risks. Participation also exposed women creators to workplace-facing surveillance. We contribute an infrastructural account of digital workplace knowledge exchange by showing how creators’ repair and maintenance labour helps sustain TikTok as an SII. This extends research on digital workplace knowledge exchange by showing that supplementary workplace knowledge can also matter for workers who remain connected to formal workplace information. The SII’s possibilities for information justice nevertheless remain uneven because they depend on creator labour undertaken under gendered and platformed conditions.

articles.title: Scripts of Escalation and Restraint: State Messaging and Public Opinion in International Crises
articles.authors: Frances Yaping Wang
articles.abstract: Public opinion can both enable and constrain foreign policy, motivating governments to manipulate media during international crises. This study identifies four recurring communication strategies, one mobilizing and three moderating, each organized around a dominant cue: mobilization relies primarily on emotional arousal to stoke nationalist sentiment and foster assertiveness; censorship centers on the informational restriction of politically sensitive content; delegitimization uses normative appeals to discredit hawkish responses as irresponsible or illegitimate; and posturing employs performative displays of toughness intended to make moderate policies politically acceptable. Using a large-scale survey experiment in China, Vietnam, and the Philippines, the study evaluates how these strategies affect the public’s foreign-policy preferences and tolerance for policy deviation in a simulated fishing dispute in the South China Sea. The results show that mobilization shifts preferences in a more hawkish direction and reduces tolerance for deviation, whereas delegitimization consistently steers the public toward more moderate foreign policy preferences across countries. Censorship tempers policy preferences in all three countries but is strongest in Vietnam; posturing has no significant effect in China or Vietnam and produces a more hawkish response in the Philippines. Although the sources of this cross-national heterogeneity cannot be definitively identified, the findings suggest that propaganda effectiveness may depend partly on how audiences interpret different messages. Explicitly prescriptive strategies, such as mobilization and delegitimization, appear more portable across contexts, whereas informational or performative strategies, such as censorship and posturing, may be more contingent on audience predispositions, including baseline hawkishness, and on broader political and informational environments.

articles.title: Attention cycles and visual frames of climate change imagery in the Vietnamese national media
articles.authors: Tuan Anh Vu, Hoai Linh Le
articles.abstract: Research on visual media representation of climate change has largely examined Western nations and paid less attention to the national media landscape in the Global South. As a highly vulnerable country to climate change and an emerging economy, Vietnam offers a critical case for exploring how visual framing intersects with institutional, cultural and geographical contexts. This study examines longitudinal trends in visual portrayals of climate change and the strategic selection of imagery through framing by Vietnamese national media. First, a content analysis was conducted on images accompanying Vietnam News Agency’s articles on climate change from 2020 to 2023 ( N = 4284). Second, a frame analysis examined the connotative and ideological representations of the most prevalent visuals to generate hypotheses about the relationship between issue attention and particular frame dominance. It was found that Vietnamese visual coverage of climate change followed a cyclical attention cycle and contributed to the prominence of the ‘government, politics and negotiation’ frame. The finding suggests relative homogeneity with global climate change coverage, except for the latent meaning in frames related to climate impacts and affected people.

articles.title: Picturing judicial authority: an investigation of visual metadiscourse on court websites of China, Britain and France
articles.authors: Min Yang, Meng Xu
articles.abstract: This study examines the visual construction of judicial authority on the websites of the Supreme People’s Court of China, the UK Supreme Court and the French Court of Cassation. Drawing on De Groot et al.’s visual metadiscourse framework (De Groot et al., ‘Picture This: Developing a Model for the Analysis of Visual Metadiscourse’, 2016), Kress and Van Leeuwen’s visual grammar and content analysis ( Reading Images: The Grammar of Visual Design , 2021[1996]), the authors develop an integrated approach to analyse how visual elements reinforce judicial authority. Additionally, Scott’s institutional legitimacy theory ( Institutions and Organizations , 1995) is employed to identify the underlying authority model of each court. Findings reveal distinct configurations shaped by divergent legal cultures: the Chinese court website reflects a state-oriented, tradition-modernity coupled model, integrating national symbols, cultural heritage and modern legal norms; the French court website presents a normative–institutional model, grounded in republican values and historical continuity; and the British court website exemplifies an historical–continuity model, rooted in tradition and the constitutional monarchy.
